title: The async handler
idea: `asyncHandler` wraps an async route handler so a rejected promise reaches `next(err)` and then the error middleware, with no `try/catch` in each controller.
points: An `async` function returns a promise; a `throw` inside it rejects that promise.
`asyncHandler(fn)` returns a handler that adds `.catch(next)` to the promise `fn` returns.
`next(err)` skips normal routes and runs the error middleware, which sends the JSON error.
Express 5 already forwards rejections itself; the wrapper also suits Express 4 projects.

steps.caption: A request reaches a route registered as `asyncHandler(fn)`. The wrapper runs first.
The wrapper calls your handler and keeps the promise it returns.
Happy path: the promise resolves after `res.json`. The wrapper has nothing more to do.
Failure path: `findUser` throws an `ApiError`, so the promise rejects and `.catch` calls `next(err)`.
`next(err)` skips the remaining routes and lands in the error middleware.
The error middleware replies with the standard error JSON and the error's status.

pitfalls: Always `await` or return promises inside a handler; a floating rejection escapes the wrapper.
Do not wrap the error middleware: the wrapper has three parameters, so Express skips it.
Never put `err.stack` or database error text in the JSON reply.

quiz.why: The rejection is handled in a microtask, after the synchronous `console.log('B')`.

takeaway: `asyncHandler` turns a rejected promise into `next(err)`: one catch, every controller.
